title: Execute sustainable resource use and quality control

lessons.title: Managing resource use sustainably
lessons.html:
Resources in production

At NQF level 4 you are expected to plan and execute operations so that resources (water, soil, energy, inputs, labour and capital) are used efficiently and without long-term damage, while the product meets quality requirements. Sustainable resource use and quality control are linked: wasted inputs and poor quality both reduce margins.

Measuring resource efficiency

Use ratios that relate resources to output, and track them over seasons and between blocks:

ResourceExample indicator
WaterCubic metres per tonne of product or per hectare; litres per animal per day
Fertiliserkg nitrogen applied per tonne yield; nutrient balance (applied minus removed)
EnergyLitres diesel per hectare; kWh per tonne cooled or pumped
FeedFeed conversion ratio (kg feed per kg gain)
ChemicalsNumber of applications per season; product cost per hectare
LabourHours or rand per tonne harvested

Executing efficient practices

  • Water: irrigation scheduling from soil moisture or evapotranspiration data; system audits for distribution uniformity; leak repairs; mulching.
  • Soil and nutrients: fertilise to soil and leaf analysis; split applications; manure and compost; erosion control; minimum tillage where suited.
  • Chemicals: integrated pest management, scouting and thresholds; calibrated sprayers; correct nozzles to reduce drift; resistance management by rotating modes of action per label.
  • Energy: pumping at off-peak tariffs where possible, maintained motors and pumps, solar options, efficient field operations.
  • Waste: compost organic waste; recycle packaging; return empty chemical containers through approved schemes.

Legal and market drivers

Conservation of Agricultural Resources Act 43 of 1983 and the National Water Act 36 of 1998 set legal obligations. Buyers increasingly audit environmental practices through GAP and sustainability schemes, so records are essential.

lessons.title: Quality control in production
lessons.html:
Quality control versus quality assurance

Quality assurance is the system that prevents problems: procedures, training and standards. Quality control is checking products and processes against specifications and acting on deviations. Both are needed.

Setting specifications

Specifications come from buyers, export standards (under the Agricultural Product Standards Act 119 of 1990 for regulated products) and the farm's own targets. Examples: size grades, colour, Brix, firmness, defect tolerances, carcass grading, milk somatic cell count and bacterial count, grain moisture and foreign matter.

Control points along the process

  1. Inputs: check seed certification, fertiliser and feed against orders and analyses; reject damaged or expired goods.
  2. Production: monitor crop or animal growth, pests and diseases, nutrition and water.
  3. Harvest: maturity tests, picking quality, handling.
  4. Post-harvest: grading, packing, cooling, storage conditions.
  5. Dispatch: labels, lot numbers, load temperature, documentation.

Sampling and inspection

Use a written sampling plan: how many units, how often and from where. Use calibrated scales, thermometers, refractometers and moisture meters. Record results on standard forms.

Using quality data

  • Calculate defect percentages and track them by block, team or day.
  • Use simple charts to spot trends.
  • Identify root causes, for example bruising traced to overfilled picking bags, or high grain moisture traced to early harvesting.
  • Take corrective action and check that it worked.

Linking quality and sustainability

Every rejected carton wastes the water, fertiliser, energy and labour used to grow it. Reducing rejects is one of the most effective ways to improve resource efficiency.

Communicating

Give teams clear standards with examples, share quality results, recognise good work and retrain where needed. Report persistent problems to management with data.

Key points

  • Measure resource efficiency with indicators like water or diesel per tonne.
  • Use scheduling, IPM, soil testing and calibration to cut waste.
  • Quality assurance prevents problems; quality control checks and corrects.
  • Sample with a plan, use calibrated instruments and record results.
  • Fewer rejects means better use of every resource.
